extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic and philosophy; logicians and scholars interested in the theory of definition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for forming and evaluating definitions of names and abstract concepts in logic and science, including distinctions between complete and imperfect definitions, modes of definition, and the relation of definitions to classification and demonstrative reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as proposition declaratory of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest and most correct notion of a Definition is, a proposition declaratory of the meaning of a word; namely, either the meaning which it bears in common acceptation, or that which the speaker or writer, for the particular purposes of his discourse, intends to annex to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A definition should state what a term means in use or for the specific discourse. It is primarily nominal (about a name's meaning), not ontological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names cannot be defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names are mere marks put upon individuals and are 'destitute of meaning,' and therefore are unsusceptible of definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to 'define' a proper name by saying e.g. 'John Thomson is the son of General Thomson' do not produce a definition; they only indicate referent. Pointing or ostension is superior for identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotative names: definition must declare connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of connotative names, the meaning is the connotation; the definition of a connotative name is the proposition which declares its connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define connotative terms either directly (stating the attributes the name connotes) or indirectly (by predicating synonymous or compound connotative names). Example forms: 'Man is every thing which possesses corporeity, organization, life, rationality...' or 'Man is a rational animal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct form is most precise but verbose
rubrics_metrics.description: The direct mode (e.g., 'Man is a name connoting such and such attributes') is the most precise and least equivocal of any; but it is not brief enough and is too technical for common discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct formulations for logical precision; use indirect/shorter forms only when brevity and common usage matter, recognizing potential loss of exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect (predicative) definitions and synonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: The more usual mode of declaring connotation is to predicate of the name another name or names of known signification (e.g., 'Man is a human being'), or several connotative names that together make up the whole connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that simple synonymy ('Man is a human being') may not be a substantive definition; compound predicates should together exhaust the connotation for completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete definition = sum total of essential propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a name is the sum total of all the essential propositions which can be framed with that name for their subject. All propositions the truth of which is implied in the name are included in the definition, if complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete definition allows evolution of all truths implied by the name without other premises; it functions as an analysis of the term's connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as analysis of constituent attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: To define is to resolve a complex whole into the elements of which it is compounded; replacing one word which connotes a set of attributes collectively by two or more which connote the same attributes singly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, break a term into its constitutive attributes (analysis). This is the preferred logical method of producing precise definitions (Condillac's view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining single-attribute abstract names via foundation phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract name expresses a single attribute (e.g., 'white' or 'rational'), the definition must have recourse to the foundation of the attribute — the fact or phenomenon from which it derives meaning — and analyze that phenomenon into parts if complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For attributes grounded in phenomena, define by describing the underlying phenomenon (e.g., 'whiteness — the property or power of exciting the sensation of white'). If the foundational experience is unanalyzable, appeal to shared sensation/experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of simple feelings are (practically) undefinable
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of simple feelings or elementary states of consciousness are unsusceptible of analysis and thus are in the same condition as proper names; their meaning cannot be unfolded by other words, requiring direct appeal to personal experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept limits: elementary mental terms may need ostensive or experiential reference rather than verbal definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between complete and popular imperfect definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people seek in a definition merely a guide to correct usage; this gives rise to 'Essential but incomplete Definitions' and 'Accidental Definitions or Descriptions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that ordinary definitions may intentionally be partial (sufficient for denotation) or descriptive (using accidents) rather than exhaustive analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential but incomplete definitions (per genus et differentiam)
rubrics_metrics.description: A connotative name may be defined by a part only of its connotation (e.g., 'Man is a rational animal'); such definitions may suffice to mark out the current denotation but are incomplete and liable to be overturned by new discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for practical discrimination, but logically incomplete. Recognize vulnerability to expanded knowledge (counterexamples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Per genus et differentiam is common but not sufficient for completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional rule that species be defined per genus et differentiam often uses only some differentiæ; a complete definition would use all attributes not already connoted by the genus ('per genus et differentias').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume a single differentia yields completeness; explicitly state any omitted attributes when precision is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental definitions (descriptions) are not genuine definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions that state attributes not in the connotation (accidents) are descriptions, rejected by logicians as genuine definitions; yet if convertible (co-extensive) with the name they can serve as correct definitions for discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing definitions on accidental features unless they are intentionally adopted as the special connotation for a purpose (see scientific/technical definitions). Check convertibility/coextensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convertibility/co-extensiveness criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition (or description raised to definition) must be convertible with the name — exactly co-extensive with it, predicable of everything of which the name is predicable and of nothing else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test candidate definitions for coextensiveness: a correct definition should neither under- nor over-extend the term's denotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/special (scientific) definitions serve classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific definitions often assign a special connotation to a common term to serve classification (e.g., Cuvier's definition of Man). Their purpose is classification rather than expounding ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining for a scientific scheme, make explicit that the definition is technical and explain the classificatory rationale; these definitions may differ from ordinary usage but must be coherent within the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific definitions are progressive and provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in the sciences are almost always technical and are constantly varying as classifications and knowledge advance; thus the definition of a science or scientific term must be progressive and provisional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scientific definitions as subject to revision; avoid rigidly tying long-term theory to transient taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions of names from definitions of things (postulate vs definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are nominal (explain the meaning of a term). What are called 'definitions of things' covertly assert existence; that assertion is not definition but a postulate. Definitions alone cannot assert the reality of a thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'means' rather than 'is' to avoid implicitly asserting existence when you only intend to set terminology. If existence or possibility is required for reasoning, state it as an explicit postulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are not premises for demonstrative reasoning without postulates
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative truths do not follow from definitions alone but from the postulates (assumptions of existence/possibility) covertly contained in some definitions; confounding these leads to error (e.g., Euclid's circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using definitions in proofs, separate the nominal content (definition) from factual assumptions (postulates). Make postulates explicit to ground reasoning legitimately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of idealized exactness in definitions/postulates
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulates or definitions in demonstrative sciences often idealize (e.g., a circle with radii exactly equal); such exactness is not realized in nature, so one must understand how much of the postulate is necessary to support the true part of a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the role of idealization: ensure that the idealized premises are adequate (but not falsely conflated with empirical fact) for the degree of truth claimed in conclusions.
